name: Alan Kay
key_figures: Smalltalk|the Dynabook|Squeak|Croquet|the Xerox PARC Learning Research Group
one_line_pitch: Computing as a medium for children and thought
description: One of the clearest voices on what computing could have been and might still become. Kay's work spans the Dynabook concept (a children's personal computer, conceived in 1972) that anticipated the iPad by forty years, the message-passing OOP of Smalltalk that influenced Objective-C and Ruby, the pedagogy of Squeak and Etoys for children, and a sustained critique of the software industry's failure to live up to its early promise. His talks ("The Computer Revolution Hasn't Happened Yet," "Doing with Images Makes Symbols," "The Future Doesn't Have to Be Incremental") are a master class in thinking about media, tools, and amplification of human capability.

name: Bret Victor
key_figures: Inventing on Principle|Dynamicland|Learnable Programming|Magic Ink|Up and Down the Ladder of Abstraction
one_line_pitch: Tools that let creators see what they are making
description: A living continuation of the Kay / Engelbart lineage. Victor argues — and demonstrates — that creators need to *see* what they are making, and that static code with numeric literals hard-coded into it is a relic of print. *Inventing on Principle* is one of the most watched talks in software; *Dynamicland* is his ongoing experiment in turning a physical community space into a shared computational medium. The essays are as carefully written as the demos are choreographed.

name: Donald Knuth
key_figures: The Art of Computer Programming|TeX|MetaFont|literate programming|Concrete Mathematics
one_line_pitch: Algorithms and typography as unified craft
description: Fifty years into TAOCP, and still the deepest treatment of algorithmic analysis ever written. Knuth also designed TeX because he wanted his book to be typeset properly, invented literate programming (code and documentation as one woven document), co-wrote *Concrete Mathematics*, won the 1974 Turing Award, and — as "Don Knuth" — plays the pipe organ. A genuinely unified aesthetic of correctness, care, and beauty applied across mathematics, typography, and software.

name: Gregory Bateson
key_figures: Steps to an Ecology of Mind|Mind and Nature|the double-bind theory|Naven|Angels Fear
primary_source: Steps to an Ecology of Mind
one_line_pitch: "The pattern which connects" across mind and nature
description: A polymath whose work reads today like a cybernetics of meaning. Bateson's "the pattern which connects" is one of the most evocative phrases in 20th-century thought; his double-bind theory shaped family therapy; his late work on the ecology of ideas anticipated Lovelock, Varela, and much of contemporary systems-ecology. He moved through anthropology, psychiatry, dolphin communication, and epistemology as though they were the same subject — because, for him, they were. The sentences themselves repay slow reading.

name: Marvin Minsky
key_figures: The Society of Mind|The Emotion Machine|K-lines|frames|Perceptrons
one_line_pitch: A modular, non-unified theory of cognition
description: Co-founder of the MIT AI Lab and one of the architects of symbolic AI. *The Society of Mind* is a modular, non-unified theory of cognition presented as 270 one-page essays — a strange and original form for a strange and original claim. Minsky was also a restless critic of neural-network orthodoxies (*Perceptrons*, with Papert) and a witty commentator on everything from Penrose's physics to Jewish mysticism. His *Emotion Machine* is a late return to the same problem from a different angle.

name: Seymour Papert
one_line_pitch: Children as scientists, learning as making
description: The great theorist of children-as-scientists. Papert studied with Piaget in Geneva before moving to MIT; his *constructionism* argues that learning is deepest when the learner constructs a shareable artifact. Logo and its turtle are the classic instantiation, but the philosophy generalizes: every Scratch, every micro:bit, every maker-space assignment owes him a debt. *Mindstorms* (1980) remains one of the most ambitious and hopeful books ever written about computers and education.

name: Rich Hickey
key_figures: Clojure|ClojureScript|Datomic|"Simple Made Easy|" "Hammock-Driven Development|" "The Value of Values"
one_line_pitch: A working programmer's philosophy of simplicity
description: Hickey designs languages for the working programmer and argues carefully for each decision. Clojure brought Lisp back into industrial relevance; Datomic rethought databases around immutable facts indexed by time; the talks are as responsible as the code for shifting how a generation of developers think about simplicity, identity, and time. "Simple Made Easy" has become canonical; "Hammock-Driven Development" is a genuinely useful piece of methodology advice.

name: Leslie Lamport
key_figures: TLA+|Paxos|"Time|Clocks|and the Ordering of Events|" Lamport clocks|LaTeX
one_line_pitch: Think before you code; mathematics as the thinking tool
description: Lamport's distributed-systems papers are so foundational that people forget he *also* gave us LaTeX. Paxos and the logical-clocks paper are indispensable; Byzantine generals formalized fault-tolerance before the term was commonplace; TLA+ is his ongoing campaign for specifying systems mathematically before coding them. His 2013 Turing Lecture argues that programmers should think before they code and that mathematics is the best thinking tool we have.

name: Brian Eno
key_figures: Ambient 1: Music for Airports|Oblique Strategies|My Life in the Bush of Ghosts|77 Million Paintings|Reflection
one_line_pitch: Music as system, creativity under constraint
description: A composer who treats music as system, not message. Eno invented "ambient" as a genre, co-created the Oblique Strategies deck with Peter Schmidt as a stuck-creator's toolkit, and produced seminal records for Bowie, Talking Heads, U2, and James. His generative apps (*Bloom*, *Reflection*, the iOS generative sound installations) are direct descendants of his systems thinking. *A Year with Swollen Appendices* and the various talks on "scenius" are primary-source generative-art theory.

name: Iannis Xenakis
key_figures: Metastaseis|Pithoprakta|the Philips Pavilion|Formalized Music|the UPIC system
one_line_pitch: Stochastic composition and architecture as one act
description: Architect, composer, engineer, and former assistant to Le Corbusier. Xenakis introduced stochastic processes, game theory, and Markov chains into musical composition; he helped design Le Corbusier's Philips Pavilion (Brussels Expo, 1958), whose ruled-surface geometry he then reused for the string-glissando score of *Metastaseis*. The UPIC system let users draw sound directly onto a graphics tablet decades before digital audio workstations did the same. *Formalized Music* remains a remarkable document: part manifesto, part mathematical appendix.

name: John Cage
key_figures: 4′33″|Music of Changes|Sonatas and Interludes for Prepared Piano|Silence|HPSCHD
one_line_pitch: Chance, silence, indeterminacy as method
description: The 20th century's most influential advocate of chance, silence, and the idea that anything can be listened to as music. Cage's collaborations with Merce Cunningham, his use of the *I Ching* to generate scores, and his writings (*Silence* especially) remade concert music, dance, and visual art alike. Love him or hate him, it is nearly impossible to do post-war music theory without him; his influence on Eno, the New York School, and most of generative art is direct.

name: Andrei Tarkovsky
one_line_pitch: Cinema as sculpture in time
description: Seven films and one book of theory; no wasted gestures in any of them. Tarkovsky's long takes, textured landscapes, and patient accumulation of time make his cinema feel closer to sculpture than to narrative. The long dolly over a swampy room in *Stalker*, the burning barn in *Mirror*, the candle scene in *Nostalghia* — each is an argument about cinematic duration. *Sculpting in Time* is among the most readable books ever written by a filmmaker about their own medium.

name: Akira Kurosawa
one_line_pitch: Frame composition and multi-viewpoint narrative
description: A master of frame composition and movement within the frame, and the filmmaker who — with *Rashomon* — taught mainstream cinema how to tell a story from multiple subjective viewpoints. Kurosawa's influence on Lucas, Spielberg, Leone, and the entire Hollywood action tradition is so direct that he is often more felt than cited. *Something Like an Autobiography* and his published storyboards (which are complete watercolor paintings) are primary-source craft material.

name: Hayao Miyazaki / Studio Ghibli
key_figures: Spirited Away|My Neighbor Totoro|Princess Mononoke|Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind|The Wind Rises
primary_source: Spirited Away, Mononoke, The Wind Rises
one_line_pitch: Hand-drawn animation with an ethics of labor
description: A body of work unified by a distinctive ethic: respect for labor, skepticism of easy morality, love of the nonhuman, and a commitment to hand-drawn animation at industrial scale. *Starting Point* and *Turning Point* (Miyazaki's essay collections) are as substantial as the films. The studio itself — co-founded with Isao Takahata and Toshio Suzuki — is a case study in sustaining craft inside a punishing industry, and the 2019 documentary *Never-Ending Man* captures the ethos.

name: M.C. Escher

Coxeter on hyperbolic tilings (Circle Limit I–IV are direct applications of Coxeter's diagrams), and his late engagement with Penrose's impossible triangle, make him a genuine bridge between fine art and formal mathematics. His prints have been over-used in kitsch, but the underlying craft is exceptional, and the drawings of regular division of the plane reward careful study.

Her essays (*Dancing at the Edge of the World*, *Words Are My Matter*) are models of critical generosity, and the 2014 National Book Award speech is still worth re-reading annually.

The smooth board-formed concrete he popularized is an entire industry's worth of imitation; the original is still quietly better than any of them.

The documentary *My Architect* by his son Nathaniel is among the best films about architecture ever made.

group_label: Group B — Specific Books & Seminal Texts

description: A father-son motorcycle trip across the American Midwest that unfolds into a sustained philosophical inquiry into *Quality* — a category that Pirsig argues precedes the distinction between subject and object. Variously classified as memoir, novel, and philosophy, the book is still a unique blend of engineering craft, Zen, Greek philosophy, and mental-health narrative. Pirsig's sequel *Lila* develops the Metaphysics of Quality more formally.

Carse distinguishes *finite games* (played for the purpose of winning) from *infinite games* (played for the purpose of continuing the play), and then uses that distinction as a lens on sex, religion, politics, war, art, and nature. Stewart Brand has called it one of the most important books he has ever read; Kevin Kelly has used it as the conceptual backbone of *The Inevitable*.

description: Companion to the four-part BBC series of the same name. A short book that permanently changes how one reads a gallery wall — essential alongside any study of photography, advertising, or visual rhetoric.

group_label: Group B — Specific Books & Seminal Texts

description: Why buildings change over time and which ones change well. Brand introduces the idea of *shearing layers of change* — Site, Structure, Skin, Services, Space plan, Stuff — moving at different rates, and argues that good architecture respects that difference. Directly applicable to software ("pace layering" has become standard vocabulary in systems architecture), institutions, and personal knowledge systems. The accompanying BBC series is out there in various forms.

name: On Growth and Form
group_label: Group B — Specific Books & Seminal Texts
one_line_pitch: Foundational mathematical biology
description: The foundational text of mathematical biology. Thompson asks why organisms take the shapes they do and answers in terms of surface tension, mechanical forces, logarithmic spirals, and affine transformations — a century before "evo-devo" was a phrase. Cited by Alan Turing in his morphogenesis paper, by Stephen Jay Gould throughout his career, and by almost everyone working in developmental biology and generative design. Thompson is already a key figure in v5's Morphogenesis topic, but the primary text itself — full of beautiful hand-drawn illustrations — is worth a slow read of its own.

name: The Road to Reality
group_label: Group B — Specific Books & Seminal Texts
one_line_pitch: All of modern physics, from fractions to twistors
description: A "complete guide to the laws of the universe," starting from fractions and ending at twistor theory, with every mathematical step supplied. Over 1,100 pages, Penrose works through complex analysis, manifolds, Lie groups, quantum field theory, and general relativity, while inserting his own heterodox views on consciousness, the measurement problem, and physical law. Either the world's most ambitious popular-physics book or the world's friendliest graduate-level reference — probably both.

name: The Design of Everyday Things
group_label: Group B — Specific Books & Seminal Texts
one_line_pitch: Affordances, signifiers, gulfs of execution and evaluation
description:
The original and still clearest treatment of affordances, signifiers, feedback, mapping, and the Gulf of Execution / Gulf of Evaluation in everyday object design. Norman's doors, stoves, and nuclear-plant control rooms taught a generation of designers that "user error" usually means "design error." Norman is cited as a figure in v5's HCI and Ecological Psychology entries; the book itself — like DDIA — rewards reading cover-to-cover on its own terms. The revised edition adds substantial material on service design and emotional design.

name: Horology & Mechanical Watchmaking

description: The art of measuring time in steel and jewels. Escapements (lever, detent, chronometer, co-axial), tourbillons, perpetual calendars, minute repeaters, striking complications, and the long rivalry between the English chronometer tradition and the Swiss jewel-watch tradition. A rare craft where the physics, the precision engineering, and the ornamental hand-finishing (anglage, Geneva stripes, black polish) are all first-class considerations. George Daniels's *Watchmaking* and Philippe Dufour's interviews are primary sources.

name: Japanese Joinery & Traditional Woodworking

one_line_pitch: Wooden structure without metal fasteners
description: Wooden buildings and furniture assembled without metal fasteners, through dozens of named joints (*kanawa tsugi*, *ari shiguchi*, *dado-nuki*, and many more). The tradition is as much about reading a specific piece of wood — its grain, moisture, species, and history — as about executing a technique. *The Art of Japanese Joinery* (Seike), *The Soul of a Tree* (Nakashima), and the documentary series on temple carpenter Tsunekazu Nishioka are good starting points.

name: Luthiery
key_figures: Stradivari|Guarneri|Antonio de Torres (guitar)|the Cremonese tradition|modern makers like Samuel Zygmuntowicz
one_line_pitch: Stringed-instrument making as physics + craft
description: Making stringed instruments — violins, guitars, cellos, lutes — is a synthesis of wood science, acoustics, geometry, and personal hand-feel. The Cremonese secret is mostly gone; what remains is two hundred years of attempted reverse-engineering, plus a new generation of computational luthiers using finite-element analysis and modal-matching. *The Strad* magazine archives and the Violin Society of America's journals document the current state of the art.

name: Letterpress, Hand Typesetting & Bookbinding
key_figures: Gutenberg|Bodoni|William Morris & the Kelmscott Press|modern fine presses (Arion|Thornwillow|the Whittington Press)
one_line_pitch: The physical substrate of typography
description: The physical substrate of what v5's Typography topic treats abstractly. Setting metal type by hand, understanding the feel of a slug of lead, binding signatures, sewing cords, gilding edges, marbling endpapers: each is a self-contained craft. Useful not just as nostalgia but as a way of understanding *why* digital typography makes the decisions it does. Bringhurst's *Elements of Typographic Style* bridges the print and digital worlds.

name: Calligraphy — Chinese, Japanese, Islamic, and Latin Traditions in Comparison
key_figures: Wang Xizhi|Ogata Kōrin|Ibn Muqla|Edward Johnston|modern practitioners
one_line_pitch: Four radically different answers to "how should writing look?"
description: Four traditions with radically different answers to the question "how should writing look?" Studied side by side, they illuminate everything: the brush vs. the reed vs. the quill; the aesthetics of the character vs. the aesthetics of the line; the relationship between script and sacred text; the role of the body, the breath, and the moment. Peter Lu's work on Islamic scripts and Shigemi Komatsu's on Japanese *kana* are fine starting points; Johnston's *Writing & Illuminating & Lettering* is the Arts-and-Crafts-era primer that still reads well.

name: Ceramics & Kiln Traditions
key_figures: Raku|Shōji Hamada|Bernard Leach|the anagama and noborigama kiln traditions|Song Dynasty celadons
one_line_pitch: Chemistry + physics + form, fired together
description: Pottery turns out to contain an enormous chemistry problem (glazes and body formulation) wrapped in an enormous physics problem (kiln firing schedules and reduction atmospheres) wrapped in a design problem (form, weight, tactility). The mingei folk-craft movement of Yanagi Sōetsu connects pottery to a whole philosophy of everyday beauty. Wood-fired anagama kilns run for days and their ash becomes part of the glaze; digitally-controlled electric kilns make entirely different aesthetic trade-offs.

name: Fermentation & Traditional Food Biotechnology
key_figures: Sandor Katz|Noma's fermentation lab|miso|koji|sourdough|kimchi|lambic beer|natural wine
one_line_pitch: Living cultures as self-sustaining systems
description: Applied microbiology with thousands of years of empirical refinement. *The Art of Fermentation* (Katz) is the readable encyclopedia; *The Noma Guide to Fermentation* is the modernist-restaurant adaptation. Connecting threads run everywhere: living cultures as self-sustaining systems; flavor as a function of microbial succession; preservation without refrigeration; the Aspergillus oryzae (koji) as the most industrially consequential fungus you have never heard of.

name: Perfumery & Olfactory Composition
key_figures: Jean-Claude Ellena|Edmond Roudnitska|Luca Turin|the Grasse tradition|modern molecular perfumery
one_line_pitch: The sense-based art with the weakest theory
description: The least theoretically mature of the sense-based arts, and therefore the most promising to think carefully about. How does a perfumer construct a three-part "accord" — top, heart, base — from dozens of volatile molecules? What is the relationship between olfactory memory and emotion? Turin's *The Secret of Scent* proposes a quantum-vibrational theory of olfaction that remains contested; Ellena's *The Diary of a Nose* is a practitioner's memoir of sustained attention.

name: Bonsai & Japanese Gardening (Karesansui)

one_line_pitch: Design at tree-time
description: Design at tree-time. Bonsai is training a tree over decades or centuries; karesansui dry-rock gardens are meditations on emptiness and composition. Both make explicit that design has a temporal dimension — the final form is the whole trajectory, not the current snapshot. The tea-garden tradition (*roji*) is a further refinement where the path to the tea house is itself choreographed to prepare the visitor.

name: Sailing & Navigation

one_line_pitch: Aerodynamics, geometry, and fatigue-decisions at sea
description: The art of moving a small vessel on the open ocean. Rigging and sail trim are a hands-on course in applied aerodynamics; celestial navigation teaches the actual geometry of the Earth (the sextant, the nautical almanac, the sight reduction tables); watch standing is a practical course in sleep, attention, and decision-making under fatigue. Slocum's *Sailing Alone Around the World* (1900) and Hiscock's *Cruising Under Sail* are primary texts; Bernard Moitessier is the philosophical edge.

name: Permaculture & Regenerative Agriculture

one_line_pitch: Living-systems design at land scale
description:
Living-systems design at the scale of a piece of land. The twelve permaculture principles, Fukuoka's *One-Straw Revolution*, Savory's holistic grazing, Shepard's restoration agriculture, and the broader agroecology literature. A direct practical application of systems thinking, ecology, and pattern-language design to the question of how humans can inhabit land productively without degrading it.

name: Linear Algebra
one_line_pitch: The substrate beneath ML, graphics, DSP, quantum
description: The mathematical substrate beneath machine learning, computer graphics, DSP, quantum mechanics, and general relativity. Matrices as linear maps, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, the singular value decomposition, tensor products, duality, and the various matrix decompositions (LU, QR, Schur, Jordan). Strang's MIT 18.06 lectures and Axler's *Linear Algebra Done Right* are the two classic on-ramps; Trefethen & Bau's *Numerical Linear Algebra* is the computational companion.

name: Real & Complex Analysis
one_line_pitch: The rigorous machinery beneath calculus
description: The rigorous machinery beneath calculus. Sequences, series, limits, continuity, differentiation, measure, integration — and then the complex plane, where analytic functions have astonishing rigidity (Cauchy's theorem, the residue theorem, the maximum modulus principle, conformal mappings). The foundation for almost all of classical applied mathematics. Abbott's *Understanding Analysis* is the gentler entry; Rudin is the rite of passage.

name: Statistics (Classical & Modern)
one_line_pitch: Inference, testing, experimental design
description: Surprisingly absent from v5 despite Probability and Machine Learning both being present. Frequentist inference, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, experimental design (factorials, blocks, Latin squares), resampling (bootstrap, jackknife, permutation tests), modern robust statistics, and the ongoing Bayesian / frequentist dialogue. Tukey's *Exploratory Data Analysis* is a rare joy; Gelman's *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel Models* is the modern applied reference.

name: Quantum Mechanics (as physics)
one_line_pitch: QM as physics, distinct from QM as computation
description: Distinct from v5's Quantum Computing topic, which is centred on qubits and algorithms. Here the focus is physical: Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures, path integrals, angular momentum, scattering, identical particles, and the interpretations (Copenhagen, many-worlds, de Broglie–Bohm pilot wave, relational, QBism). Feynman's *Lectures on Physics* Volume III remains a top-tier introduction; Sakurai's *Modern Quantum Mechanics* is the graduate-level standard.

name: Cosmology & Astrophysics
key_figures: Weinberg|Peebles|Martin Rees|Penrose|the Planck|JWST|LIGO|Event Horizon Telescope eras
one_line_pitch: The outward scale from Relativity
description: The outward scale from Relativity. General-relativistic cosmology, ΛCDM, inflation and its alternatives, the cosmic microwave background, dark matter and dark energy, stellar nucleosynthesis, black holes and gravitational waves. Weinberg's *The First Three Minutes* and Rees's *Just Six Numbers* are the classic popular entries; Peebles is the technical standard; *The Road to Reality* (Group B) is a useful companion.

name: Cell & Molecular Biology
key_figures: Alberts et al. (Molecular Biology of the Cell)|James Watson|the central dogma|modern single-cell sequencing
one_line_pitch: The substrate on which evolution operates
description: The substrate on which evolution actually operates. DNA replication, transcription, translation; membrane biology; the cell cycle; signaling networks; the gigantic biochemical machines (ribosomes, proteasomes, spliceosomes) that do the routine work of cellular life. Alberts's textbook is the standard; Molecular Biology of the Gene (Watson et al.) is the complementary gene-focused view; Larry Gonick's *Cartoon Guide to Genetics* is a surprisingly good popular warm-up.

name: Immunology
key_figures: Janeway's Immunobiology|Susumu Tonegawa|Paul Ehrlich|the innate vs. adaptive systems|modern checkpoint therapies
one_line_pitch: Self/non-self recognition as computation
description: The study of self / non-self recognition at a molecular level — arguably the most explicitly computational system in biology. Antibody generation through V(D)J recombination, T-cell receptor diversity, HLA matching, inflammation, tolerance, autoimmunity, and vaccine design. An entire distributed information-processing system living inside every vertebrate, with pattern recognition, memory, and clonal-selection dynamics built in.

name: Paleontology & Deep Time
key_figures: Stephen Jay Gould|Neil Shubin|Richard Fortey|the Burgess Shale|the five great mass extinctions
one_line_pitch: The actual timescale evolution inhabits
description: The actual timescale evolution inhabits. Stratigraphy, radiometric dating, fossil reconstruction, punctuated equilibrium, the major transitions in evolution (Cambrian explosion, the Devonian colonization of land, the K-Pg extinction, the rise of mammals and primates). Fortey's *Life: A Natural History of the First Four Billion Years* is a lovely single-volume tour; Gould's *Wonderful Life* remains essential on the Burgess Shale; Shubin's *Your Inner Fish* is the pop accessible entry.

name: Climate Science & Earth Systems
key_figures: IPCC reports|James Lovelock (Gaia hypothesis)|Johan Rockström (planetary boundaries)|Syukuro Manabe
one_line_pitch: Systems thinking at civilizational stakes
description: Large-scale systems thinking at civilizational stakes. Radiative forcing, the carbon cycle, ocean–atmosphere coupling, ice sheet dynamics, climate-sensitivity estimates, the planetary-boundaries framework, and the political economy of decarbonization. Essential to understand both as physics and as governance problem. The IPCC Working Group reports are surprisingly readable given their size; David Archer's *Global Warming: Understanding the Forecast* is a fine single-volume primer.

name: Political Philosophy
one_line_pitch: What legitimates authority and justifies justice?
description: From *The Republic* to *A Theory of Justice*, the Western tradition's sustained attempt to answer a small set of hard questions: what legitimates political authority? what is justice? what do citizens owe each other? The 20th-century debates between Rawls and Nozick, and the communitarian critique from MacIntyre and Sandel, remain live and directly relevant to contemporary AI governance and platform economics. Overlaps with Greek Philosophy but deserves its own sustained thread.

name: Ethics (Consequentialism / Deontology / Virtue)
one_line_pitch: Three normative traditions, applied to an AI era
description: The three main normative traditions, their internal varieties, and the meta-ethical questions about whether moral claims are true, objective, or reducible. Applied ethics — bioethics, environmental ethics, AI ethics — flows directly from these foundations. Parfit's *Reasons and Persons* is among the most rigorous pieces of moral philosophy ever written; Williams's *Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy* is the sharp critique from the other side.

name: Existentialism
one_line_pitch: Meaning, authenticity, freedom, finitude
description: The Western tradition's sustained argument with itself about meaning, authenticity, freedom, and finitude. Kierkegaard's "leap of faith," Nietzsche's revaluation of values, Heidegger's *Being and Time*, Sartre's "existence precedes essence," Camus's absurd, de Beauvoir's ethics of ambiguity. A natural counterpoint to Eastern Philosophy, a deep prerequisite for Phenomenology, and still unusually readable compared to most academic philosophy.

name: Psychoanalysis
one_line_pitch: The structure of the unconscious (distinct from v6 Jungian track)
description: Distinct from v6's *Comparative Mythology & Depth Psychology*, which is framed around Jung and Joseph Campbell. Classical psychoanalysis proper is concerned with the structure of the unconscious, drives, repression, dream-work, transference, and the clinical setting. Lacan's linguistic turn ("the unconscious is structured like a language") deserves particular attention for its influence on structuralism, critical theory, and film studies.

name: Developmental Psychology
one_line_pitch: How minds assemble over time
description: How minds assemble over time. Piagetian stages, Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, attachment theory, temperament, theory-of-mind development, and Tomasello's work on shared intentionality as the origin of human cognition. Essential for understanding Seymour Papert's constructionism and for anyone designing for children or building learning systems.

name: Flow & Positive Psychology
one_line_pitch: A psychology of flourishing, not just of deficit
description: A psychology concerned with what makes lives flourish rather than with what makes them fail. Flow (total absorption in challenge-matched activity), character strengths, gratitude, resilience, meaningful engagement. The field has internal debates about rigor (the replication crisis has been unkind to parts of it), but the core findings on flow in particular are a useful bridge from cognition to craft practice — and from clinical-deficit models of the mind to capability-building ones.

name: Japanese Aesthetics
key_figures: Yanagi Sōetsu (The Unknown Craftsman)|Tanizaki (In Praise of Shadows)|Okakura Kakuzō (The Book of Tea)|Zeami
one_line_pitch: wabi-sabi, mono no aware, yūgen, ma as a unified theory
description:
A unified theory assembled across centuries of poetry, tea ceremony, Noh theatre, pottery, ink painting, and architecture. *Wabi-sabi* (beauty of imperfection and impermanence), *mono no aware* (the pathos of transient things), *yūgen* (profound mystery), *ma* (negative space), *iki* (sophisticated restraint), *shibui* (astringent beauty). Tanizaki's *In'ei Raisan* is a fine literary distillation; Donald Keene's surveys are the scholarly entry.

Active research on this frontier is unusually public; the LessWrong and Alignment Forum archives are primary source material.

The research programme attempts to reverse-engineer what trained networks actually compute, bottom-up, through individual components rather than via behavioral probing. Still young as a field but already producing fine-grained results on small-to-medium language models and vision models.

name: Synthetic Biology & CRISPR-era Genetics
key_figures: Jennifer Doudna|Emmanuelle Charpentier|George Church|Drew Endy|Craig Venter|the iGEM competition
one_line_pitch: Engineering life
description: Engineering life. CRISPR/Cas gene editing, prime editing, base editing, gene drives, synthetic genomes, designer microbes for drug and materials production, xenobots, and the nascent field of "living materials." Questions span the technical (delivery, off-target effects, immunogenicity), the ecological (gene drives in the wild, population-level impact), and the ethical (germline editing, de-extinction, the limits of consent).

name: Brain-Computer Interfaces & Spatial Computing
key_figures: Neuralink|BrainGate|Synchron|Meta Reality Labs|Apple Vision Pro|the Sutherland tradition
one_line_pitch: Where phenomenology and hardware meet
description: Where phenomenology and hardware meet. Invasive vs. non-invasive BCIs (microelectrodes, ECoG, EEG, fMRI, MEG, fNIRS), motor imagery decoding, speech synthesis from cortical signals, and the convergence with AR/VR into "spatial computing." Raises serious questions about embodiment, agency, privacy, and the limits of first-person experience — and is beginning to deliver real clinical results for locked-in patients.

name: Prediction Markets & Epistemic Infrastructure
key_figures: Robin Hanson|Manifold|Polymarket|Kalshi|the Good Judgment Project|Philip Tetlock
one_line_pitch: Forecasting as a civic tool
description: Forecasting as a civic tool. The theory of prediction markets (information aggregation, incentive compatibility, manipulation-resistance, liquidity dynamics) and the practice (what actually happens when you run one at scale, including the politics of which contracts are legal where). Superforecasting, calibration training, scoring rules. An under-appreciated branch of collective intelligence work, still establishing its institutional form.

name: Longtermism & Existential Risk Studies
key_figures: Nick Bostrom|Derek Parfit|Toby Ord (The Precipice)|William MacAskill|Owen Cotton-Barratt|the Future of Humanity Institute and CSER
one_line_pitch: The normative frame for civilizational thinking
description: The normative claim that the long-term future matters morally, and the empirical study of what could prevent humanity from having one. Asteroid impacts, engineered pandemics, unaligned AI, great-power nuclear war, engineered totalitarianism. Philosophically contested (population ethics is hard; strong longtermism has prominent critics), but the research programme has become institutionally serious in the past decade.

name: Digital Commons & Platform Economics

one_line_pitch: Commons theory meeting the modern internet
description:
Ostrom-style commons theory meeting the modern internet. The governance of digital commons (Wikipedia, open-source software, open scientific knowledge), platform monopoly dynamics, algorithmic labor markets, data commons and data trusts, and the ongoing legal and political contest over what "public infrastructure" means in a fully online economy. Zuboff's *Surveillance Capitalism* is the critical pole; Benkler's *Wealth of Networks* is the constructive pole.
